section_summary: This section documents Japanese public finance during 1930–1931, including refinancing of a maturing sterling loan, successive national and colonial budgets, expenditure reductions, unemployment relief, and the government's increasingly strained no-loan policy. A substantial group of papers concerns the London Naval Treaty, the division of anticipated naval savings between fleet replenishment and tax relief, and public criticism that naval demands would frustrate promised reductions in taxation. The section concludes with correspondence about United States methods of issuing national debt, further Japanese budget cuts, and the beginning of a November 1931 report on the budget, borrowing, and the gold embargo.

subfiles.title: File note on removal of the Japanese gold embargo
subfiles.about: Records a cross-reference to a despatch concerning the removal of Japan's gold embargo and immediate gold withdrawals.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Neville's Despatch 1393; about ¥100,000 in gold withdrawn the first day after the embargo was lifted.

subfiles.title: File note on refinancing Japan's sterling loan and the naval conference
subfiles.from: London Naval Conference; Henry L. Stimson
subfiles.about: Summarizes the relationship between Japanese participation in a naval treaty and refinancing a ¥240 million foreign loan.
subfiles.summary: A four-percent sterling loan of about ¥240 million was due for refunding January 1, 1931; bankers would favor it if Japan joined the naval treaty but might withhold funds if it rejected it.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting proposed Japanese external-loan terms
subfiles.about: Reports press accounts of negotiations for refinancing Japan's sterling loan after conclusion of the Naval Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Japan's London fiscal agent opened talks after the Naval Treaty on a ¥250 million loan at 5.5 percent for thirty years, yielding about 6.2 percent, with Parr's, HSBC, Rothschild, National City and others reported as underwriters.

subfiles.title: Undersecretary's memorandum approving the Japanese bond issue
subfiles.about: Records Cotton's approval of a Japanese bond issue after interdepartmental consultation.
subfiles.summary: Cotton approved the Japanese bond issue after consulting Secretary Lamont and Assistant Treasury Secretary Hope, who consulted Mellon, and told Leffingwell of J. P. Morgan by telephone.

subfiles.title: J. P. Morgan & Co. letter describing the Japanese Government external loan
subfiles.to: Joseph P. Cotton, Undersecretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides the proposed structure and underwriting arrangements for bonds refunding Japan's 1905 sterling loan.
subfiles.summary: J. P. Morgan describes refunding the £25 million 1905 sterling loan, about £23.5 million outstanding due January 1, 1931, via a $50 million American offering of 5.5 percent bonds in a $71 million issue plus £12.5 million in London.

subfiles.title: Typed copy of J. P. Morgan & Co.'s Japanese bond letter
subfiles.to: Joseph P. Cotton, Undersecretary of State
subfiles.about: Reproduces the Morgan firm's explanation of the proposed Japanese refinancing issue.
subfiles.summary: Typed copy of Morgan's letter repeating the bond terms, the American syndicate, simultaneous London offering and conversion bonds.

subfiles.title: Cotton memorandum on preliminary discussion with J. P. Morgan & Co.
subfiles.about: Reports an initial oral inquiry concerning Japanese borrowing in London and New York.
subfiles.summary: Cotton says Morgan discussed floating a Japanese bond issue to refund earlier obligations; he did not commit the Department but saw no reason to object to Japanese borrowing in the US.

subfiles.title: Economic Adviser's memorandum on mishandling the Morgan loan inquiry
subfiles.about: Explains why the Morgan firm's written inquiry about the Japanese loan received no formal written reply.
subfiles.summary: Economic Adviser's memo: Morgan followed its oral inquiry with a letter routed to Cotton's office but not the Economic Adviser, though Cotton had already told Leffingwell of no objection.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 188 transmitting Japan's supplementary budget for 1930–1931
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Transmits and analyzes the Japanese supplementary budget for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1931.
subfiles.summary: Neville explains that dissolution of the Diet prevented passage of the regular budget, leaving the government to operate largely under prior appropriations supplemented by new votes. He compares Seiyukai and Minseito budgets, emphasizing retrenchment from ¥1.773 billion to about ¥1.609 billion while identifying appropriations for education, unemployment relief, industrial rationalization, trade, and other programs. The enclosure gives detailed ordinary and extraordinary revenues and expenditures, continuing appropriations, special accounts, colonial administrations, and supplementary estimates totaling approximately ¥40.7 million.

subfiles.title: File note and attached report on Japan's budget outlook for 1931–1932
subfiles.about: Discusses fiscal difficulties in drafting Japan's next budget and reductions in the current working budget.
subfiles.summary: Press anticipated a major 1931-1932 revenue decline making the no-loan policy hard to keep; Hamaguchi would retain it while allowing local relief borrowing; about ¥60.5 million in reduced or deferred spending was secured after War and Navy negotiations.

subfiles.title: File note on proposed fisheries appropriations
subfiles.about: Lists fisheries items in the Agriculture and Forestry Department's draft estimates.
subfiles.summary: Proposed fisheries appropriations: ¥80,000 for the Russo-Japanese Fishery Convention, ¥100,000 for southern-sea fisheries, plus whaling and small-port equipment.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 16 on the London Naval Treaty, taxation, and naval replenishment
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes Privy Council approval of the London Naval Treaty and the political dispute over using naval savings for replenishment or tax relief.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports unanimous Privy Council approval and recounts Viscount Ishii's criticism of the Navy's asserted fundamental principles and proposed replenishment program. He argues that the Japanese public had been led to expect meaningful tax relief and that unemployment and falling revenue made extensive naval spending politically hazardous. Enclosures reproduce the Privy Council committee's report and a Japan Advertiser article containing statements by Foreign Minister Shidehara and Premier Hamaguchi on peace, national security, and lighter public burdens.

subfiles.title: File note on insurance-company lending in Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on Japanese insurance companies lending money to domestic companies.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 38 on insurance in Japan, explaining why insurance companies were lending to Japanese firms.

subfiles.title: File note on Japan's five-year naval replenishment program
subfiles.about: References a despatch commenting on a newly announced five-year Japanese naval program.
subfiles.summary: Proposed naval replenishment program of about ¥505 million over five years; underlying despatch comments.

subfiles.title: Handwritten abstract of the forthcoming Japanese budget
subfiles.about: Summarizes expected reductions and selected appropriations in the draft budget for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1931.
subfiles.summary: Abstract: the budget was about ten percent below the working budget and fourteen percent below the previous year, with big Navy, War and Foreign Affairs cuts.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 50 on Japan's draft budget for 1931–1932
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the Cabinet-approved Japanese budget for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1931.
subfiles.summary: The draft totaled about ¥1.448 billion and was the smallest Japanese budget since 1923, reflecting depressed revenues, the absence of a carried surplus, proposed tax reductions, and adherence to the no-loan policy. Forbes compares departmental allocations with three earlier budgets and lists notable projects in foreign affairs, domestic administration, defense, industry, agriculture, education, overseas affairs, and finance. Critics argued that tax relief and unemployment provisions were inadequate and that more of the savings from the London Naval Treaty should benefit taxpayers.

subfiles.title: File note on allocation of London Naval Treaty savings
subfiles.about: Records an agreement dividing anticipated naval-treaty savings between the Navy and tax reduction.
subfiles.summary: Of about ¥505 million released by the London Naval Treaty, ¥373 million went to naval purposes and the rest to tax cuts, with another ¥25.8 million earmarked for the navy.

subfiles.title: File note and estimates for the Japanese and colonial budgets, 1931–1932
subfiles.about: Presents rough national and colonial budget estimates for the 1931–1932 fiscal year.
subfiles.summary: 1931-1932 estimates: revenue about ¥1.459 billion, expenditure ¥1.449 billion, surplus ¥10.2 million; colonial budgets for Korea, Formosa, Kwantung, Saghalien and the South Seas total about ¥406.7 million.

subfiles.title: File note and memorandum on loans under the Road Loan Law
subfiles.about: Reports Home Office instructions governing local loans for road construction and unemployment relief.
subfiles.summary: On January 12 the Home Office instructed chief surveyors in all prefectures concerning flotation of loans under the Road Loan Law. The proceeds were intended to improve roads while providing employment.

subfiles.title: Treasury letter explaining United States national-loan procedures
subfiles.about: Supplies information requested by Kakutaro Suzuki on how the United States issues and refunds national debt.
subfiles.summary: Treasury explains US bonds, notes, certificates and bills, mostly issued at fixed prices except competitively bid bills, with Treasury offices and Federal Reserve Banks as fiscal agents and no agent fees; encloses circulars.

subfiles.title: Suzuki inquiry on the flotation of United States national loans
subfiles.from: Kakutaro Suzuki, Imperial Japanese Government Financial Commission
subfiles.to: William S. Broughton, Commissioner of the Public Debt
subfiles.about: Requests information about the methods, machinery, fees, and exchange terms used in United States government borrowing.
subfiles.summary: Suzuki asks whether US national loans are sold at fixed prices, by bids or privately, which institutions take part, agents' pay, and rebates on exchanges.

subfiles.title: State Department note forwarding its reply to the Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards for Treasury information a copy of the note transmitting its May 26 letter to the Japanese Ambassador.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State sends the Treasury a copy of the note to the Japanese Embassy transmitting its explanation of national-loan practices.

subfiles.title: State Department note transmitting Treasury information to Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits the Treasury Department's response for delivery to Kakutaro Suzuki.
subfiles.summary: State encloses the Treasury's May 26, 1931 letter on flotation of US national loans for the Japanese Ambassador to forward to Suzuki in New York.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy acknowledgment of the Treasury information
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt and forwarding of the Treasury letter on United States national loans.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Ambassador thanks the Secretary for the June 4 note and confirms the Treasury letter went to Kakutaro Suzuki.

subfiles.title: File note on Hoover's moratorium and Japan's international debts
subfiles.about: References a memorandum on Japan's minor international debt entanglements under President Hoover's moratorium.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: statistics on Japanese intergovernmental and relief debts under Hoover's moratorium and the January 20, 1930 Hague reparations agreement.

subfiles.title: File note and report on proposed Japanese budget cuts
subfiles.about: Describes resistance by government departments to Finance Ministry reductions in the forthcoming budget.
subfiles.summary: Finance Ministry sought ¥54 million in savings but other departments, especially the Army, accepted only about ¥35.1 million; with a deficit of at least ¥60 million, balancing the budget might threaten the government.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 379 on Japan's budget and gold embargo
subfiles.doc_type: cross-reference sheet with partial despatch copy
subfiles.about: Introduces a financial-affairs despatch discussing the budget, possible new borrowing, and the gold embargo.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 379 fragment: speculation the government might abandon its no-loan policy for ¥30-40 million in loans; revenue expected to fall about ¥100 million, notably sake and income taxes.
